The snippet you provided shows “Table 1.1: BRIC elements – supported features” from the FEX-DYN manual. Below is a structured, detailed description of that table, suitable for ingestion into a RAG/vector store:

1. Table Title  
   • “Table 1.1: BRIC elements – supported features”

2. Purpose and Context  
   • This table summarizes which numerical and physical features are available for three types of brick continuum (“BRIC”) elements in the FEX-DYN explicit‐dynamics kernel.  
   • BRIC elements are 3D continuum elements used for spatial finite‐element meshes; they are fully integrated to avoid hourglass modes and can be run under small‐displacement (1st‐order) or large‐displacement (3rd‐order) formulations.  

3. Column Definitions  
   – 8-node BRIC  
     • A hexahedral element with eight corner nodes.  
   – 6-node BRIC  
     • A pentahedral (wedge) element with six nodes.  
   – 4-node BRIC  
     • A tetrahedral element with four nodes.  

4. Row Definitions (features)  
   1. Number of integration points  
      – 8-node BRIC: 8  
      – 6-node BRIC: 8  
      – 4-node BRIC: 1  
      • Indicates the number of Gauss integration points per element.  
   2. Fully integrated formulation  
      – Checks (✓) in all three columns.  
      • All BRIC elements here are fully integrated to suppress zero‐energy (hourglass) modes.  
   3. Hourglass‐stabilization via non-conforming shape functions  
      – Checks (✓) in all three columns.  
      • Zienkiewicz‐type shape‐function modifications are applied to prevent locking and hourglassing.  
   4. First‐order (small‐displacement) kinematics  
      – Checks (✓) in 8- and 6-node; also ✓ in 4-node.  
      • All element types support the linear (small‐displacement) formulation (equilibrium in the undeformed configuration).  
   5. Third-order (large-displacement) kinematics  
      – Checks (✓) in 8- and 6-node; (✓) also shown for 4-node.  
      • All three element types can be used in the nonlinear, large‐displacement setting (equilibrium in the deformed configuration).  
   6. Anisotropic or advanced material models  
      – Checks (✓) in all three columns.  
      • Each element supports the full suite of material models available in FEX-DYN (including hyperelasticity, plasticity, etc.).  

5. Key Observations  
   – The 8-node and 6-node BRIC elements share an identical set of capabilities; they differ only in the element topology.  
   – The 4-node BRIC (tetrahedron) has a single integration point, making it less accurate per element but still supports all integration and nonlinearity features.  
   – By fully integrating all elements and employing non-conforming shape functions, FEX-DYN mitigates hourglass instabilities without resorting to reduced integration.  
   – Users can select among these element types based on mesh geometry and desired accuracy:  
     • Hexahedra (8-node) for regular grids, best accuracy.  
     • Wedges (6-node) for transitional zones.  
     • Tetrahedra (4-node) for meshing complex geometries.  

6. Implications for Modelers  
   – When building dynamic explicit analyses under FEX-DYN, choosing the appropriate BRIC element balances accuracy, computational cost, and mesh flexibility.  
   – The uniform support of both small‐ and large‐displacement theories allows seamless transition from linear to fully geometric‐nonlinear simulations without changing element type.  

This description captures the structure and intent of Table 1.1, mentally cross‐referencing the manual’s discussion on BRIC elements in Section 1.2.2 and ensures that key numerical and formulation details are clearly identified for downstream retrieval.

   – Purpose: To show at a glance which of the listed computational features (rows) are available for each of the three one-dimensional element types (columns) when used in FEX-DYN’s explicit-dynamics kernel.

2. Column Headings (Element Types)  
   a) TRUS (Truss elements)  
   b) CABL (Cable elements)

3. Row Headings (Supported Features)

      – “Small displacements; equilibrium formulated in the undeformed configuration.”  
   2) 3rd order theory  
      – “Large displacements and large deformations; equilibrium formulated in the deformed configuration.”  
   3) Elastic material behaviour  
      – “Linear elastic stress–strain relationship.”  
   4) PRE, GAP, YIEL, CRAC  
      – “Special nonlinear material/contact behaviors:  
         • PRE (pre‐tensioning or initial stress)  
         • GAP (opening/closing contact behavior)  
         • YIEL (plastic yielding)  
         • CRAC (crack growth or fracture‐mechanics extension)”

4. Check‐Mark Entries  
   – A check mark (✓) in the intersection cell indicates that the corresponding feature is implemented for that element type.  
   – From the table, all features listed in the rows are supported by all three element types:
     • 1st order theory: ✓ under TRUS, CABL, SPRI  
     • 3rd order theory: ✓ under TRUS, CABL, SPRI  
     • Elastic material behaviour: ✓ under TRUS, CABL, SPRI  
     • PRE, GAP, YIEL, CRAC: ✓ under TRUS, CABL, SPRI  

5. Interpretation and Context  
   – Truss elements (TRUS) and cable elements (CABL) differ conceptually—cables cannot support compression—but both can be treated in small- or large-displacement regimes within FEX-DYN’s explicit solver.  
   – Spring elements (SPRI) are purely one-dimensional connectors that can also exhibit the same theoretical formulations and material behaviors.  
   – The uniform set of check marks illustrates that the software developers have provided a consistent implementation of first- and third-order kinematics and a shared library of elastic and selected nonlinear material/contact models (PRE, GAP, YIEL, CRAC) across all three element types.  
   – Users who need to model pre-stressed trusses, gap-closing cables, yield behavior in springs, or crack propagation in any of these elements can rely on FEX-DYN’s internal routines without resorting to external subroutines.

6. How This Fits Into the Manual  
   – Immediately preceding the table, Section 1.2.2 describes the overall family of spatial continuum and line‐type elements, numerical integration (hourglass control), and avoidance of locking via non-conforming shape functions.  
   – The hint box below the table reminds users that all implemented 3D finite elements carry only three translational degrees of freedom per node; beam‐type elements with rotational DOFs are not yet supported by FEX-DYN.

By consolidating the capabilities for truss, cable, and spring elements into one feature matrix, Table 1.2 offers an at-a-glance reference for modelers to confirm that the element formulations and material/contact options they require are available within SOFiSTiK’s FEX-DYN module.

 Introduction
 What to expect from this tutorial?
 This tutorial is intended to provide a first introduction into the program and to demonstrate the usage of the program with the help of simplified as well as more complex examples. It is not intended to be a substitute for the program manual.
 Several different examples ranging from the analysis of the simply supported beam to nonlinear analysis of the box girder bridge under earthquake excitation with uplifting bearings are treated.
 The input files for all the examples can be found in dyna.dat/english/fex folder.
 The underlining theory (mechanics and FEM technology) will, within the framework of this tutorial, be explained only up to a level which is necessary for understanding the examples and for correct usage of the program.
 1.2 FEX-DYN - Program Features
 1.2.1 Introduction
 FEX-DYN is a FEM analysis kernel for the explicit integration of the equations of motion within a SOFiSTiK family of programs. FEX-DYN is efficiently programmed to cope with the physically and geometrically non-linear problems and conceptualized for the usage on a multiprocessor machines (parallel computing). During the computation all the data necessary for the current time step computation are kept completely in RAM.
 1.2.2 Finite Elements
 At the moment primarily spatial continuum elements with different number of nodes are avail- able (Fig. 1.1). The input and mesh generation are, as usual, performed with the help of SOFiMSHA, SOFiMSHC or SOFiCAD. In order to avoid numerical instabilities (hour glass modes) all the elements are fully integrated. To prevent potential locking problems non- conforming shape functions according to Zienkiewicz [1] are used.
 The elements can be used for the calculations according to the theory of first order (small dis-
 placements; formulation of the equilibrium in the unreformed configuration) as well as accord- ing to the third order theory (large displacements - in particular large deformations; formulation of the equilibrium equations in the deformed configuration) (Table 1.1).

The elements can be used for the calculations according to the theory of first order (small dis-. placements; formulation of the equilibrium in the unreformed configuration) as well as accord- ing to the third order theory (large displacements - in particular large deformations; formulation of the equilibrium equations in the deformed configuration) (Table 1.1)..
 In addition truss and cable elements as well as the springs are available for the calculation (Fig. 1.1).
 Truss and cable elements can be calculated according to the 1st or 3rd order theory. These elements posses no internal nodes between two end nodes, to describe for example the cable slack effects. For the description of cable slack effects one should use several cable elements. In contrast to truss elements, the cable elements are not able to resist pressure forces. Addi- tionally the spring elements are available for the calculation with FEX-DYN (Table 1.2).
 Hint
 All implemented finite elements in the 3D calculations posses only three displacement degrees of freedom (, , ) per node. For example in a spatial calculation of the beam elements there are (at least) three additional rotational degrees of freedom. These ele- ments are not yet supported by FEX-DYN.

For the description of the material behaviour of the continuum elements all the linear and non- linear material models available in SOFiSTiK are available for FEX-DYN as well.
 Truss, cable and spring elements support features such as pre-stress (PRE), gap in connection elements (GAP), yielding in tension and in compression (YIEL) as well as the rapture (CRAC).

At the moment the static and dynamic point, area and volume loads including the self- weight can be used. The loads are conservative. Deformation-depended, external loads are currently not supported. The loads from temperature, creep and shrinkage, which are typically defined trough specification of strains, are not yet supported as well.

The explicit integration of the equation of motions requires calculation with many small time steps. The size of the time step depends of the element size (stability criteria): The smaller the elements (edge lengths) are, the smaller the chosen time step must be in order to perform a numerically stable calculation.
 In certain cases, for example in case of an earthquake analysis, in which the external loading is defined as discrete function with certain time resolution, it makes sense to specify a particular size of the time step. In many cases however the user wants to use the largest time step size possible, in order to limit the total computational time. Based on the element edge lengths FEX- DYN determines the critical time step size for the particular calculation model automatically.
 Hints for the meaningful modelling, time step and element sizes, as well as the expected com- putational times are given in the Chapter 5.

sections: 2 Explicit Integration of the Equations of Motion - Simply Supported Beam
2.1 Statement of the Problem

content:
The figure presents the basic geometry of a straight, uniform beam of length l = 10 m that is simply supported at both ends. Visually, the beam itself is drawn as a single straight horizontal line. Directly beneath the left and right ends of that line are two identical triangular symbols, each representing a support that restrains vertical displacement but allows free rotation (i.e. classical pinned or roller supports).  

Key graphical elements and annotations:  
1. Beam span line  
   - A long horizontal line denotes the beam’s neutral axis, extending from left support to right support.  
2. Support symbols  
   - Two isosceles triangles under the beam ends  
     • Left triangle marks the origin of the beam’s local coordinate x.  
     • Right triangle marks the opposite simply supported end.  
   - These symbols imply vertical reaction forces at the ends but no moment resistance.  
3. Coordinate arrow  
   - Immediately to the right of the left support, a small horizontal arrow labeled “x” points toward the right.  
   - This establishes the positive x-axis along the beam’s longitudinal direction, with x = 0 at the left support and x = l at the right.  
4. Length dimension  
   - A straight dimension line beneath the beam connects the two support bases.  
   - Midway along that dimension line is the label “l = 10 m,” indicating the clear span between supports.  
5. Caption  
   - Below the diagram is the text “Figure 2.1: Geometry of the simply supported beam,” identifying the illustration in context.

Although not shown directly in the sketch, the accompanying problem statement specifies that the beam is made of reinforced concrete with Young’s modulus E = 30 000 MN/m² (i.e. 30×10⁶ kN/m²) and mass density ρ = 2500 kg/m³. Its constant cross-section has area A = 0.5 m², giving a mass per unit length μ = ρ A = 1250 kg/m. The bending stiffness EI is then calculated as 312 500 kN m².  

In the analytical setup that follows this figure, the beam is modeled using the Euler–Bernoulli assumptions (neglecting shear deformations and rotary inertia), so its vibrational behavior in the fundamental mode depends solely on that flexural rigidity EI and the span l. The diagram thus serves as the geometric foundation for deriving the beam’s natural angular frequency (ω₁ ≈ 49.35 rad/s) and period (T ≈ 0.127 s) in purely bending vibration.

In order to start the computation, DYNA is called with the following input:

CTRL OPT RLC controls from which load case number (here VAL 1000) the results are stored. The V2 parameter controls then which results are to be saved. There is no adjustment of the number of the time steps in a sense that the total computational time would be kept constant, even in case when the time step size is changed.

The figure presents a time‐history plot of the midspan displacement (in millimeters) at node 1005 of a structural model, charted over a 1.6-second interval. The horizontal axis is labeled “time [s]” and runs from 0.0 s to 1.6 s in 0.2 s increments, while the vertical axis is labeled “displacement [mm]” and spans from 0 mm at the baseline up to 12 mm in steps of 2 mm. A fine gray grid overlays the plotting region to aid visual reading of both axes.  

Superimposed on this grid is a single, smooth black curve that describes a nearly sinusoidal oscillation of the midspan point. At t = 0 s, the displacement starts at zero, then rises to its first peak of just over 10 mm at roughly t = 0.1 s. It subsequently crosses back through zero before reaching a negative or near‐zero valley, and repeats this cycle continuously over the full duration. There are approximately 14 to 15 complete oscillation cycles visible between 0 and 1.5 s, implying a dominant frequency on the order of 9–10 Hz (period ≈ 0.1 s).  

Although the envelope of the waveform appears almost constant in amplitude, a very slight downward drift may be discerned—peak displacements toward the right side of the plot (around 1.4 s) are marginally less than the 10.2 mm seen during the early cycles. This subtle reduction in peak height is consistent with a lightly damped system, in which energy is removed slowly over many cycles.  

In the context of FEX-DYN’s damping formulations (Rayleigh and modal), this response likely reflects a mass-proportional (“diagonalized”) damping treatment. If Rayleigh damping were used, the plot was generated using a constant factor RADA computed by RADA = 2·D·ω, where D is the user-specified damping ratio and ω the angular frequency of the excited mode. Alternately, under modal damping, the software would internally estimate ω and simply apply 2·D·ω to the diagonal mass terms without requiring the user to supply the natural frequency explicitly.

• A single, solid black line  tracing the oscillatory motion.  
• Uniform grid background with both major and minor grid lines.

2.4 Damped Vibrations (D=5%)
2.4.1 Background

content:
FEX-DYN uses exclusively a diagonalized, mass proportional damping, which can be defined either as a Rayleigh and/or as a modal damping.
 For the Rayleigh damping the mass vector (i.e. diagonalized mass matrix) is multiplied with a fixed, constant factor which is specified by the user. For the expected, predominately exited vibration mode and its corresponding angular frequency ω one can compute this Rayleigh factor as:
 RADA = 2 · D · ω ,
 (2.7)
 where D is the (viscous) damping ratio.
 For the modal damping a similar factor is used, with a difference the user does not have to worry about the estimation of the exited eigenfrequency but the program approximately determines the natural angular frequency by itself, and the user only needs to provide the damping ratio.

The call for DYNA calculation for the free, damped vibrations is practical the same as for the previous example, except that here additionally the damping is specified via GRP record.
 In the following input block the command GRUP RADA 2*0.05*49.348 defines a 5% damping, where it is assumed that the beam will oscillate with the natural angular frequency of ω = 49.348rd/s.
 +PROG DYNA
 HEAD Explicit Integration - damped - Rayleigh A CTRL OPT RLC VAL 2000 V2 1 GRP MODD 0.0 RADA 2*0.05*49.348 STEP N 15000 DT 0.0001 INT 100 THE 0.0 LC NO 2 DLZ 1.0 END
 GRP MODD @.@ RADA 2x*0.05*49.348
 Alternatively one can specify the damping as the modal damping with a command GRUP MODD 0.05:
 +PROG DYNA
 . . . GRP MODD 0.05 RADA 0.00 . . . END
 The input of both the Rayleigh and the modal damping will result in a additive damping. There- fore is the other value, for clarity sake, here explicitly set to zero.
 In order to be able to compare the results of different calculations, the results are saved in the database from LC 2000 (STEU OPT ELF WERT 2000) and LC 3000 ( STEU OPT ELF WERT 3000).

The image is a high-resolution, two-dimensional line plot entitled “Figure 2.4: History of the midspan (node 1005) displacement [mm] over time [s]”. It shows the transient response of a damped single-degree-of-freedom system under a constant external load. Key features of the plot are:

1. Axes and Grid  
   • Horizontal axis (abscissa): time from 0 to 1.6 s, marked every 0.2 s. Labels use a comma as the decimal separator (e.g. “0,2”, “1,4”).  
   • Vertical axis (ordinate): displacement in millimetres from 0 to 12 mm, marked every 2 mm.  
   • Light grey grid lines create a regular rectangular mesh to aid in reading off values.

2. Oscillatory Trace  
   • The curve begins at the origin (0 s, 0 mm), then rapidly rises to its first positive peak of approximately 9.55 mm at around 0.08 s.  
   • It crosses downward past the static equilibrium displacement of about 5.15 mm and reaches a first trough of roughly 1.5 mm at ∼0.15 s.  
   • Subsequent peaks occur at diminishing amplitudes—second crest ≈8.2 mm at ∼0.23 s, third crest ≈7.4 mm at ∼0.30 s, etc.—and the troughs likewise rise toward the equilibrium line.  
   • By about 1.2 s, the oscillations have decayed to small fluctuations about the 5.15 mm level, indicating that most kinetic energy has been dissipated by viscous damping.

3. Damping Characteristics (Contextual Notes)  
   • The static equilibrium (under constant external load) is at 5.15 mm; amplitudes are measured relative to this offset.  
   • Logarithmic decrement δ was obtained from two successive peak amplitudes (first peak ≈9.55 mm and second ≈8.37 mm relative to equilibrium) as  
      d = ln(9.55 − 5.15) – ln(8.37 − 5.15) ≈ 0.312.  
   • Viscous damping ratio ζ = δ / (2π) ≈ 0.0498.  
   • The damped natural angular frequency ωd can be expressed as  
      ωd = sqrt(ω₀² – (d/(2m))²),  
     but for small damping (ζ ≪ 1), ωd is almost equal to the undamped natural frequency ω₀.

4. Behavioral Interpretation  
   • The rapidly decaying envelope illustrates underdamped vibration: the system oscillates freely around the shifted equilibrium until energy is exhausted.  
   • Each cycle’s amplitude decrement is nearly constant in logarithmic scale, confirming linear viscous damping assumptions.  
   • After roughly 10–12 cycles (about 1.2 s), the motion is effectively “settled” and the structure rests at its new equilibrium under load.

Overall, the plot provides a clear visual of time-domain decay in an underdamped mechanical system, illustrating how successive peaks diminish according to the computed logarithmic decrement and damping ratio until the static equilibrium position is reached.

content:
Apart from dynamic the program is capable of calculating static problems as well. In this case the behaviour of the structure under damped vibration conditions is exploited in a sense that a oscillation of damped system converges to a static equilibrium position. In order to keep the computational costs (equivalent to the number of time steps) to a minimum, it is optimal for the system to be in the dynamic relaxation state, i.e. damped with critical damping.
 The corresponding input file is similar to those previously used.
 +PROG DYNA
 HEAD Dynamic Relaxation CTRL OPT RLC VAL 5000 V2 1 GRP MODD 1.0 RADA 0.0 STEP N 5000 DT 85 INT 100 THE 0.0 LC NO 5 DLZ 1.0 END
 HEAD Dynamic Relaxation
 The results are saved in the load cases starting from LC 5000 (CTRL OPT RLC VAL 5000).
 To set up dynamic relaxation the damping is selected close to the the critical damping; here the damping is set to 100% of the critical damping (MODD 1.0). Good results - in sense of the short computation times - can be usually achieved with values for the critical damping between 0.85 and 0.90.
 In dynamic relaxation calculation die kinetic energy is, as with any damped oscillation, succes- sively reduced. The computation is terminated when either the actual kinetic energy in one time step is smaller than 1.0E − 15 times the maximal kinetic energy or when the maximal number of the times steps is reached.
 For this example the program requires less than 5000 time steps. Therefore one can input STEP N 5000. Otherwise the end static equilibrium state might not be exactly reached, in case when the number of time steps N is too small and this criteria determines the end of the calculation.
 Generally it is recommended to specify sufficient number of time steps, so that the program does not terminate the computation due to a limited number of time steps. In case of prelimi- nary test on a new, unknown system, it makes sense to limit the number of the time steps to reduce the computation time. In any case one should verify if the kinetic energy at the end of the calculation has been dissipated and the static equilibrium position is reached.

In case of prelimi- nary test on a new, unknown system, it makes sense to limit the number of the time steps to reduce the computation time. In any case one should verify if the kinetic energy at the end of the calculation has been dissipated and the static equilibrium position is reached..
 In order to reach the static equilibrium one has to calculate approximately one period of oscil- lation T. Therefore one should choose the time step size as large as possible, but not larger than critical time step size. In order to make the choice of the time step size easier for the user, the program offers the possibility to automatically determine the maximum theoretical time step size, depending on the geometry of the FE mesh.
 With DT 85 the time step of 85s will not be used (physically reasonable time step sizes are in the range of milliseconds!), but the program is instructed to set the actual time step size to be 85% of the theoretical possible time step size. This input is valid whenever DT is set to be larger than 1.0.

The provided Table 2.1 is part of a study comparing two computational approaches—ASE (presumably an analytical or semi-analytical static‐equilibrium solver) and FEX (the DYN-FEX dynamic relaxation solver at load case LC 5036)—for predicting out-of-plane displacements of a symmetric structural half-model. Below is a detailed breakdown of its structure, contents and key take-aways in the context of the surrounding discussion.

1. Table Layout and Headings

   • FEX columns (“u_y[mm]” and “u_z[mm]” for LC 5036)  
     – u_y[mm]  : Corresponding transverse displacement from the DYN-FEX dynamic relaxation solution at load case 5036.  
     – u_z[mm]  : Corresponding out-of-plane displacement from DYN-FEX.

2. Numerical Data and Trends  
   – Node 1: ASE and FEX both predict zero displacement in y and z, indicating either a fixed support or symmetry boundary.  
   – Node 1001: A small transverse displacement (0.0225 mm) coupled with a modest out-of-plane deflection (1.6136 mm).

       • p_gen = 79.575 (unit unspecified, but consistent across analyses)

4. Key Takeaways for a RAG Vector Store

   – Consistency: Perfect numerical agreement between ASE (static) and FEX (dynamic relaxation).  
   – Trend: Displacements grow monotonically with node index, reflecting increasing bending or deflection along the structural span.

content:
Here is a structured, field-by-field description of “Table 2.2: Load-time function” suitable for ingestion into a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store. It covers each column’s meaning, data type, units, and the way this table integrates into the FEX-DYN input deck.

1. Table Name and Purpose  
   • Name: “Table 2.2: Load-time function”  
   • Purpose: Defines a piecewise-linear time-history of an external load multiplier to be applied in a dynamic analysis. In this example the load is half the self-weight scaled by the factor F(t).

2. Column Definitions  
   A. Column 1  
     – Header label: T [s]  
     – Full name: Time (seconds)  
     – Data type: Floating-point  
     – Unit: seconds (s)  
     – Role: Independent variable. Specifies key instants at which the load multiplier is defined. The program linearly interpolates F between these times.

   B. Column 2  
     – Header label: F [–]  
     – Full name: Load multiplier (dimensionless)  
     – Data type: Floating-point  
     – Unit: dimensionless (–)  
     – Role: Dependent variable. Multiplies the reference load (here, half the self-weight). For t>0.2 s this equals 2.0, so the applied load is 1.0×self-weight.

3. Rows (Data Points)  
   – Row 1:  
     • T = 0.0 s, F = 1.0  
     • Initial condition: At the start (t=0), the load equals 1.0×(self-weight / 2).  
   – Row 2:  
     • T = 0.2 s, F = 2.0  
     • End of ramp-up: Load grows linearly from 1.0 to 2.0 over the first 0.2 s yielding a trapezoidal shape.  
   – Row 3:  
     • T = 1.0 s, F = 2.0  
     • Hold period: From t=0.2 s through the end of analysis at 1.0 s, the load remains constant at 2.0.

4. Relationship to Input Deck  
   In the SOFiLOAD preprocessing block, this table corresponds to the FUNK definition:  
     “FUNK T 0.0 F 1.0; 0.2 2.0; 1.0 2.0”  
   This discrete definition directs the trapezoidal load-time curve (Fig. 2.5). During the DYNA stage, LC=6 references this load case, and the solver applies it over 10 000 time steps (DT=0.0001 s) up to 1.0 s, storing results every 100 steps (0.01 s intervals).

5. Interpolation Behavior  
   • Between T=0.0 s and T=0.2 s: F(t) increases linearly from 1.0 to 2.0.  
   • From T=0.2 s onward until T=1.0 s: F(t) remains constant at 2.0.  
   • Before t=0 or after t>1.0 s: No further points defined; behavior depends on solver defaults (often zero or constant extension).

6. Usage Notes and Metadata  
   • Damping (10%) is set separately via “GRP RADA 2*0.1*49.348” in the DYNA input.  
   • Reference to self-weight: F=2.0 actually corresponds to 2 × (0.5 × self-weight) = 1.0 × self-weight.  
   • Critical time step remark: If the user-supplied DT (0.0001) exceeds the internally computed critical Δt, FEX-DYN will auto-adjust unless overridden by a percentage command.

By breaking down the table into its semantic components, units, interpolation rules and links to the solver commands, this description supports precise retrieval and accurate prompt responses in any RAG-powered workflow.

As in the standard DYNA model, in FEX-DYN time-varying loads in form of a load case with a corresponding time function can be defined and calculated.
 In this example we want to apply the external load with a trapezoidal load-time function (instead of a suddenly applied rectangular load-time function as in the Section 2.3 and subsequent ones) to a damped system (D = 10%).
 The load-time function starts at t = 0 with ƒ(0) = 1.0, then grows linearly until t = 0.2s where it reaches the value of 2.0. After that the load-time function stays constant (Fig. 2.5). As a load a half of the self-weight is taken so that the loading for times t > 0.2s has an amplitude of a 1.0 times self-weight.
 The load-time function is defined with SOFiLOAD. The definition of the loading starts by the definition of a LC load block, in which, as usual, the loads are defined. After that corresponding load-time function is defined with FUNK T 0.0 F 1.0; 0.2 2.0; 1.0 2.0. This defines a discrete set of function values (Tab. 2.2) which are linearly connected to give a load-time function shown on Fig. 2.5.
 +prog sofiload head Dynamic Loading $$ lc no 6 dlz 0.5 type none titl 'f(t)' func t 0.0 f 1.0; 0.2 2.0; 1.0 2.0 $$ end
 $$

 We want to perform the calculation up to 1.0s. Since the critical time step size is larger than 0.0001s, we can use this time step size and calculate 10000 time steps (STEP N 10000 DT 0.0001). With STEP INT 100 we instruct the program to store the results of every 100th time step, or in other words the results at every 100 · 0.0001 = 0.01s will be available.

 With GRUP RADA 2*0.1*49.348 a 10% damping is defined.

The image is a two‐dimensional line chart (Figure 3.3) plotting how the total number of time steps required by a dynamic relaxation solver to reach a static equilibrium state depends on the value of externally applied modal damping D (expressed as a percentage). Major features of the chart are as follows:

• Axes and Grid  
  – Horizontal axis (x-axis): “External damping in %” running from 0 % on the far left up to 100 % on the far right, with tick marks (and grid lines) at 0 %, 20 %, 40 %, 60 %, 80 %, and 100 %.  
  – Vertical axis (y-axis): “Number of required time steps” ranging from 0 at the bottom to 16 000 at the top, with major ticks (and horizontal grid lines) every 2 000 steps (0, 2 000, 4 000, …, 16 000).  
  – Both axes use linear scaling and light gray grid lines to aid reading intermediate values.

• Data Series  
  – Seven data points are shown at damping values of approximately 40 %, 50 %, 60 %, 70 %, 80 %, 90 %, and 100 %. Each point is marked by a hollow white circle outlined in black.  
  – These markers are connected by a solid black line, forming a characteristic “U”-shaped curve.

• Numerical Trend  
  – At 40 % damping the solver takes about 4 200 time steps to converge.  
  – As damping increases to 50 %, the required steps drop to a minimum of roughly 3 300 steps—the fastest convergence in this example.  
  – Beyond 50 %, further increases in D lead to a sharp rise in the required step count:  
     • ~6 800 steps at 60 %  
     • ~8 800 steps at 70 %  
     • ~10 400 steps at 80 %  
     • ~12 000 steps at 90 %  
     • ~13 600 steps at 100 %  
  – The upward trend beyond 50 % indicates that overly large external damping actually slows the dynamic relaxation process.

• Caption  
  – Directly beneath the chart is the figure caption: “Figure 3.3: Dependency of the number of required time steps of the external damping in %.”

Contextually, the chart illustrates that in material‐nonlinear simulations with plastic behavior, the convergence speed of a dynamic relaxation method depends on the total (external + internal) damping. Internal damping stems from plastic hysteresis. Even though critical damping (D = 1.0 or 100 %) might accelerate convergence in purely linear systems, here the curve shows a clear optimal region near 50 % external damping. Below 50 %, insufficient damping allows residual vibrations and slight unloading during the load application, causing divergence from the true static solution; above 50 %, excessive damping unduly slows the relaxation process. Overall, this plot provides guidance for selecting an external modal damping ratio that minimizes computational time without introducing spurious dynamic effects.

 Looking at previous examples one could expect that if an external modal damping which is closer to a critical one (D = 1.0) is used, the convergence of a dynamic relaxation will be faster. In case of a material non-linear calculations, in particular with plastic material behaviour, this does not necessary hold because due to the plastic material behaviour an additional in- ternal material damping is present. It can be observed that for a choice of D = 50% (or less) the computed static equilibrium state diverges from the exact solution due to the fact that the dynamic computation results in a unwanted vibrations. The material is no longer only monotonously loaded but also during the process of loading in part also unloaded (hysteresis).

    – From t = 0 onward, the graph displays a straight line sloping downward from (0, r₀) to a point labeled (t_d*, 0) on the time axis.  
    – This linear interpolation models the gradual reduction in overpressure as the shock wave attenuates. The assumption of linear decay is a simplification intended for static structural analysis rather than a full dynamic blast‐wave simulation.

 3. Positive Pressure Duration (t_d*):  
    – The intersection of the decay line with the time axis occurs at t = t_d*, marking the end of the positive‐phase of the blast load. Beyond this point, the pressure is assumed to return instantly to ambient (zero gauge overpressure) for the purposes of the static‐equivalent loading model.  
    – In more detailed explosive‐loading models, a negative (suction) phase may follow, but it is omitted here.

 4. Contextual Simplifications:  
    – The triangular pulse shape (constant slope) is widely used in structural blast engineering for hand calculations or simplified finite‐element load cases.  
    – In the accompanying façade‐beam study, this pulse is converted into an equivalent uniform horizontal line load p (kN/m) over the beam span—derived from the planar overpressure acting on the façade area between adjacent support beams.

How this ties back to the façade‐beam analysis:

  • The reflection peak overpressure r₀ and the positive impulse (area under the p(t) curve) are first computed from fundamental blast parameters. In the example, an impulse parameter r = 1,062.9 Pa·s was used.  
  • The triangular time history is then collapsed into a static, equivalent distributed load on the simply supported beam. With a façade panel spacing of 6.0 m and two faces (front and back), the effective line load becomes p_line ≃ 972.6 kN/m.  
  • This approach allows the structural analyst to apply a single, constant horizontal load in a linear‐elastic or elastoplastic beam model rather than performing a full transient dynamic simulation.

In summary, the diagram streamlines a complex blast‐wave process into a first‐order, triangular‐pulse representation defined by its peak r₀ and its duration t_d*. This serves as the foundation for converting dynamic blast effects into an equivalent static loading scenario on the façade beam.

content:
The figure is a two-dimensional line plot of the beam’s horizontal midspan displacement versus time, labeled “4.4: Time history of the horizontal midspan displacement of the beam.” It shows a single continuous, smooth curve without discrete markers, plotted on a rectangular grid with evenly spaced horizontal and vertical grid lines.

Axes and scaling  
• X-axis runs from 0.00 to 0.16 (presumably seconds), with ticks at 0.02 s intervals.  
• Y-axis runs from 0 to 140 (presumably millimeters of horizontal displacement), with ticks every 20 units.  
• Both axes are linear and unlabeled directly with units on the figure, but context indicates time in seconds and displacement in millimeters.

Key features of the curve  
1. Initial rise (loading to free vibration transition)  
   - From t = 0 s the displacement starts at 0 mm, increasing rapidly during the dynamic loading phase (t = 0 to ≈ 0.013 s).  
   - The curve reaches its first and highest peak of about 120 mm at roughly t = 0.02 s, occurring well after the external load has already dropped to zero.  
2. Free‐vibration decay around a new mean  
   - After the first large overshoot, the structure enters free vibration.  
   - The response oscillates between troughs of approximately 60 mm and peaks near 100 mm.  
   - The mean of these later cycles appears to lie around 80 mm, reflecting the permanent plastic deformation that shifts the equilibrium position.  
   - The amplitude of oscillation decays only modestly from the first to the second cycle (≈±20 mm about the new 80 mm mean) and remains nearly constant through at least four half-cycles (up to t ≈ 0.14 s).  
3. Damped sinusoidal character  
   - The shape of the oscillations is roughly sinusoidal but with slight asymmetry (e.g., the first half-cycle is steeper than later ones).  
   - There is a clear decay in amplitude very quickly from the first peak to the second trough, after which the amplitude stabilizes, consistent with material (internal) damping being activated once plastic deformation occurs in the flanges.  

Interpretation in context  
• The first peak corresponds to the maximum bending displacement under high-dynamic load.  
• The time of this maximum (≈0.02 s) is well after the load application phase (t = 0 to 0.013 s).  
• Once the beam’s flanges in the midspan plastify, the internal damping increases and rapid decay of the first oscillation occurs.  
• The later cycles oscillate around a shifted equilibrium (~80 mm permanent displacement), showing smaller, more uniform amplitudes as the structure vibrates in a new plastic-deformed state.

Overall, the plot clearly conveys (a) the peak horizontal displacement under dynamic loading, (b) the activation of plastic deformation and associated damping, and (c) the free‐vibration response decaying into oscillations around a permanently shifted midspan position.

content:
The figure is a stress–strain plot for a single finite‐element “flange” (element 196) taken from the midspan of an I-beam under dynamic loading.  Its key features are as follows:

1. Axes and grid  
   • Horizontal axis: engineering strain in the beam‐length (z) direction, expressed in percent. Tick marks and gridlines appear at 0 %, 5 %, 10 %, 15 %, 20 %, 25 %, and 30 %.  
   • Vertical axis: von Mises (edge‐tension) stress in MN/m², ranging from –600 to +600 MN/m², with major gridlines every 200 MN/m².  
   • The origin (0 %, 0 MN/m²) sits in the lower left quadrant where the two axes meet.

2. Initial loading branch (thin line, near‐horizontal top path)  
   • Starting at (0, 0), stress rises almost linearly with strain up to roughly 3–4 % strain, reaching a stress level just over 400 MN/m².  
   • Once yield stress is attained (around 420 MN/m²), the curve flattens into a long plateau (plastic flow region), extending from about 5 % strain all the way to nearly 28–30 % strain at a nearly constant stress of 430–450 MN/m².  
   • This plateau corresponds to the beam’s plastified flange section, as noted by the extensive red‐colored area in the companion contour plots.

3. Hysteresis (reversal) loops (thicker, more vertical segments)  
   • After the first load reversal (free‐vibration phase), the stress–strain trajectory detaches from the plateau and follows a steep unloading path toward negative stresses.  
   • The unloading branch is nearly parallel to the initial elastic loading slope but shifted rightward by roughly 20 % strain—this horizontal shift reflects the permanent (plastic) deflection of approximately 80 mm that defines the beam’s new equilibrium point.  
   • The curve reaches a negative stress extreme near –500 to –550 MN/m² at about 20–22 % strain.  
   • Subsequent reloading then tracks back up in compression (still plastic), forming a narrow hysteresis “diamond” loop. Small deviations from perfect linearity in the flow branch are visible; these are attributed to three‐dimensional effects within the finite‐element system.

4. Post‐hysteresis elastic branch  
   • Beyond the plastic reversal loop, the final part of the curve settles onto a smaller, elastic unloading/reloading path, roughly parallel to the original slope, indicating that most further oscillations occur within the elastic range around the shifted zero‐stress point.

5. Interpretation in dynamic context  
   • The thick looped lines correspond to the time history captured at node 1350 (with strain approximated by displacement differences between nodes 1350 and 1349, divided by the element length).  
   • The wide plateau confirms that the flange region has yielded and plastified during the high‐dynamic loading phase (t ≈ 0.002 s to 0.013 s), with peak bending displacement occurring at t ≈ 0.02 s.  
   • Internal (material) damping activates once plastic deformation begins, so free‐vibration amplitudes decay faster than during the loading phase, and the curve quickly relaxes into the shifted elastic hysteresis loop around the new permanent deflection.

In summary, this plot vividly illustrates (a) linear elastic response up to yield, (b) extensive plastic flow plateau, (c) pronounced hysteresis during the first load reversal, and (d) a final elastic branch around a permanently shifted zero‐stress reference—behavior that underpins the beam’s dynamic plastic deformation under impact‐type loading.

5.1 Statement of the Problem

content:
The input table (Table 5.1) gathers the key elastic‐dynamic properties of two materials—concrete and steel—used in the bridge model. These properties feed directly into the estimate of the explicit‐time‐integration critical time step via the compression‐wave velocity. Below is a column‐by‐column breakdown, followed by an interpretation in the context of the earthquake simulation.

1. Table Title  
   “Typical compression wave velocities for concrete and steel.”

2. Columns and Units  
   • Material: identifies the solid (concrete or steel).  
   • E [kN/m²]: Young’s (elastic) modulus, given in kilonewtons per square meter.  
   • ν [–]: Poisson’s ratio (dimensionless), describing lateral contraction under axial load.  
   • ρ [t/m³]: Mass density in metric tons per cubic meter (1 t/m³ = 1 000 kg/m³).  
   • c [m/s]: Computed compression‐wave (dilatational) velocity in meters per second.

3. Table Values  
   a) Concrete  
     – E = 3.0 × 10⁷ kN/m² (i.e. 30 GPa)  
     – ν = 0.20  
     – ρ = 2.500 t/m³ (2 500 kg/m³)  
     – c = 3 650 m/s  

   b) Steel  
     – E = 2.1 × 10⁸ kN/m² (i.e. 210 GPa)  
     – ν = 0.30  
     – ρ = 7.850 t/m³ (7 850 kg/m³)  
     – c = 6 000 m/s  

4. Underlying Formula  
   The compression‐wave velocity c is obtained from the linear elastic relation (Eq. 5.1), which for isotropic media may be written in a compact form as  
   c = √[E(1 − ν) / ρ(1 + ν)(1 − 2ν)]  
   The numbers in the table are the result of inserting the respective E, ν, and ρ values into that expression.

5. Role in Explicit Dynamic Analysis  
   – In an explicit finite‐element scheme, stability requires that the time step Δt be smaller than the critical time step controlled by the fastest wave speed and the smallest element length (l_min):  
     Δt_max ≈ l_min / c  
   – Using the concrete velocity c ≈ 3 650 m/s and the estimated minimal element edge of roughly 0.2 m (plate thickness direction), one obtains a Δt on the order of 5.4 × 10⁻⁵ s.  
   – This Δt ensures that the simulated pressure (compression) waves do not “skip” across elements in one step, avoiding numerical instability.  
   – Given an 8 s earthquake record, some 150 000–200 000 time steps are required to cover the loading and immediate post‐shock behavior.

6. Practical Implications  
   – Since concrete is significantly more compliant (lower E) and lighter (lower ρ) than steel, it exhibits a lower wave speed. The steel bridge bearings or reinforcement will thus carry compression impulses faster.  
   – The choice to mesh plates and shells with a single element through the thickness relies on the BRIC element’s ability to capture both bending and shear. The table’s velocities nevertheless govern the global time‐step constraint, not the in‐plane discretization alone.  
   – All subsequent estimates of total computational time (≈ 2 024 s on the given hardware for 200 000 steps) rest on the Δt dictated by the values in this table.

In sum, Table 5.1 provides the foundational elastic‐dynamic parameters needed to size both the spatial mesh and the temporal resolution for a stable, accurate explicit dynamic simulation of the bridge under the chosen earthquake excitation.

The table “Table 5.2: Critical time step sizes for different structural elements of the horizontal bridge-earthquake model” summarizes, for each key component of the finite-element mesh, (1) its representative thickness, and (2) the maximum stable time increment Δt when using an explicit integration scheme.  In explicit dynamic analyses the global time step must not exceed the smallest elemental time step dictated by the local wave‐propagation speed and characteristic element dimension.  Here the critical Δt values were obtained by first computing the compression‐wave velocity v from equation (5.1) (which combines Young’s modulus E, Poisson’s ratio ν, and density ρ), and then taking the element’s minimal edge length—as approximated by its thickness in this one‐element‐through‐thickness model—divided by v.  

Columns  
• Bauteil: name of the structural element in the bridge model (in German).  
• Dicke [m]: nominal thickness of that element, which here serves as the characteristic length for wave travel.  
• Δt [s]: the corresponding critical time step in seconds, i.e. the largest increment that ensures numerical stability in an explicit time‐integration of the equations of motion.  

Rows (elements)  
1. Fahrbahnplatte (Deck slab)  
  • Dicke = 0.25 m  
  • Δt = 6.85 × 10⁻⁵ s  
  – The road/deck slab is relatively thin, but because concrete’s wave speed is high, its critical time step is on the order of 10⁻⁵ s.  

2. Stege (Webs or ribs)  
  • Dicke = 0.50 m  
  • Δt = 1.37 × 10⁻⁴ s  
  – The thicker ribs allow a larger time step—about twice that of the deck—since the element dimension is doubled.  

3. Bodenplatte (Base slab)  
  • Dicke = 0.20 m  
  • Δt = 5.40 × 10⁻⁵ s  
  – The base slab is the thinnest element modeled and thus controls the global time step (smallest Δt).  

Key implications for the bridge seismic analysis:  
• Global time step: the smallest Δt in the table (5.40 × 10⁻⁵ s) sets the upper bound for all elements in the explicit integration—any larger increment would violate the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy stability condition.  
• Total number of time steps: to capture an approximately 8 s long earthquake record (San Francisco 1957, dt = 0.02 s, resampled internally), one requires at least 8 / 5.4e-5 ≈ 150 000 steps; a margin was added to reach 200 000 steps for post-excitation observation.  
• Mesh size and computational cost: with 840 plate/shell elements in the girder and 1 184 elements in the two piers (2024 total), and an explicit performance of ~200 000 element-time-steps/s on a reference Intel Core i5 platform, the full 200 000 steps require about  
  200 000 steps × 2024 elements / 200 000 elem·steps/s ≈ 2024 s (≈33.7 min).  

By documenting these Δt values alongside each element’s defining dimension, the table provides a concise reference for modelers to balance spatial discretization, numerical stability, and run time when setting up nonlinear, fully time-integrated earthquake simulations of single-span bridge systems.

5.1 Statement of the Problem

content:
Nowadays more and more single span bridge systems are built in the earthquake prone zones. For these structures in case of different horizontal stiffness of adjacent peers, e.g. due to differ- ences in peer heights or differences in ground conditions, it can happen that, under horizontal earthquake excitation, the bridge experiences torsional effects.
 In the initial state the bridge girder is in the contact with all four supports. During an earthquake due to high torsional loads significant tensile forces can occur on individual bearings. Due to structure design of various bridge bearings a vertical uplifting (tensile) force usually cannot be transferred. Within a framework of a linear earthquake analysis (e.g. integration of equations of motion using modal superposition or linear time history calculation) these (positive) effects can not be taken into an account. In order for these and other non-liner effects to be taken into consideration within a dynamic analysis, the equations of motion must be (fully) non-linearly integrated.
 d = 0.25 m
 The bridge is supported on two peers, with heights of 17.10m and 22.10m.
 The bridge is exited by a horizontal earthquake, in the direction normal to the bridge axis. The acceleration time history of the San Francisco earthquake from 22.3.1957 ( station: Alexander Building NO-9-W) is used. The acceleration time history is recorded at each dt = 0.02s. The duration of the earthquake is approx. 400 · 0.02 = 8 seconds (Fig. 5.2).
 Before starting with the creation of a finite element model, prior to the analysis of the mesh size in the light of the expected results and in the light of the model size, the computation time and the scope of the results should be addressed.
 The computation times depend always on the type of the problem and can only be estimated approximately in advance. Apart from the actual computation, a significant part of the compu- tation time is needed for the output of the results in the output files and the data base. The main part of the computational effort is spent for the computation of the stresses in each indi- vidual BRIC element and the integration of the internal nodal forces per each time step.  The system definition takes place in SOFiMSHA. As usual, the rotational degrees of freedom are suppressed with SYST FIX MM.
 FEX-DYN supports the standard kinematic coupling used by other SOFiSTiK modules. The horizontal displacements of the bridge girder and the peers are coupled together. For example the following input defined the coupling of the displacement degree of freedom in the x-direction of the node 4095 (KINE ND 4095 FIX PX) with the displacement in the x-direction of the node 35 (ND1 35.1 FD1 1.0):

The image is a two‐dimensional, grid‐backed line plot labeled as “Fig. 5.3: Time history of the vertical bearing force of the truss No. 1 during a linear and non‐linear analysis.” Along the horizontal axis the time runs from 0.0 s up to 10.0 s, marked in one‐second increments. The vertical axis shows the bearing force in kilonewtons (kN), ranging from –8000 kN at the bottom to +4000 kN at the top, with tick marks every 1000 kN. A gray, evenly spaced Cartesian grid underlies the plot, aiding in visual comparison of the two curves.

Two overlaid curves illustrate the comparison between linear and non‐linear model results. A black dashed line traces N_linear [kN], while a solid black line traces N_non-lin [kN], as indicated by the legend positioned inside the plot area (lower‐right quadrant).  

Phase 1 (0–2 s): Both curves begin at around –2000 kN and exhibit small, low‐frequency oscillations of similar amplitude. They remain closely aligned, indicating almost identical compressive bearing forces under both linear and non‐linear assumptions when no uplift or impact has occurred.  

Phase 2 (2–6 s): Around 2 s a clear divergence appears. The dashed (linear) curve swings into positive tensile territory, peaking near +2500 kN, whereas the solid (non-linear) curve is “cut off” at zero tension—flattening whenever the linear model predicts uplift. Shortly thereafter, at roughly 3 s, a pronounced negative spike in the non‐linear case plunges toward –7500 kN, signifying an impulsive compressive rebound as the bridge girder impacts its bearings. This event also injects high‐frequency oscillations into the non‐linear response, seen as rapid, densely packed fluctuations in the solid line. The linear model likewise oscillates but with lower frequency and gentler amplitude.  

Phase 3 (6–10 s): Past 6 s both curves settle into a decaying sinusoidal pattern of diminishing amplitude. External damping attenuates the high‐frequency content in the non‐linear response, causing both solid and dashed lines to re‐converge. By 10 s they track each other closely around zero force, demonstrating that after the transient impact the non‐linear system behavior aligns once again with its linear counterpart.  

Overall, the graph visually conveys how tension cutoff and impact‐induced oscillations in the non‐linear analysis create marked deviations from the linear solution during mid‐phase, followed by re‐synchronization under damping in the final seconds.

The image presents “Figure 5.4,” an enlarged view of axial‐force time‐histories for a bridge girder between t = 2.0 s and t = 6.0 s, comparing linear and non-linear analyses. It is rendered on a Cartesian grid with horizontal and vertical gridlines:

• X-axis: time in seconds, marked at 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0, 5.5, and 6.0 s.  
• Y-axis: axial force in kilonewtons, with major ticks at –8000, –6000, –4000, –2000, 0, 2000, and 4000 kN.  

A dashed line traces N_linear [kN], and a solid line traces N_non-lin [kN]. The curves begin at approximately –4000 kN (compression) at t = 2.0 s and display pronounced oscillations throughout the interval:

1. 2.0 s to 2.5 s – Both models exhibit similar initial troughs and peaks around –3000 kN to –1000 kN.  
2. ≈2.6 s – The linear response (dashed) spikes upward sharply to roughly +2500 kN, whereas the non-linear response (solid) remains near zero, illustrating the “cut-off” of tensile forces once uplift and clearance occur.  
3. 2.7 s to 3.2 s – The linear curve swings between +1500 kN and –7000 kN with high amplitude; the non-linear curve shows damped, narrower oscillations confined between about –2000 kN and +500 kN.  
4. 3.5 s to 4.5 s – Both traces continue oscillating, but the non-linear response displays high-frequency “ringing” immediately after the girder impacts the piers, then decays faster due to the enforced gap and nonlinear contact behavior.  
5. After ≈5.5 s – The two curves converge and nearly overlap, indicating that external damping has attenuated the high-frequency content and the non-linear system behavior aligns closely with the linear prediction.

Context notes (not shown on the plot): the full dynamic run required about 2100 s of CPU time on an Intel Core i5/M460 dual-core at 2.53 GHz with 4 GB RAM under Windows 7 SP1. The figure illustrates how non-linear contact (uplift and re-impact) truncates tensile forces, injects high-frequency energy upon re-contact, and ultimately yields a response that, after transient effects subside, parallels the linear model’s behavior.
